ref: 2 Apol. 6 (Otto and ANF chapter numbering; no sub-sections marked in the Greek)
greek: Ὁ δὲ υἱὸς ἐκείνου, ὁ μόνος λεγόμενος κυρίως υἱός, ὁ λόγος πρὸ τῶν ποιημάτων καὶ συνὼν καὶ γεννώμενος, ὅτε τὴν ἀρχὴν δι᾽ αὐτοῦ πάντα ἔκτισε καὶ ἐκόσμησε,
greek_edition: Otto 1842 vol. 1, read from the PDF page image (pdftoppm, 110-120 dpi) and cross-checked with the OCR text layer; OCR-era accents on function words not independently checked. Verbs: συνὼν (pres. part. of σύνειμι, 'being with'), γεννώμενος (pres. part. pass. of γεννάω, 'being begotten'), πρὸ τῶν ποιημάτων ('before the creatures'), ἔκτισε ('created'). Otto's note says γεννᾶσθαι is Justin's 'solemn verb' for this.
english: And His Son, who alone is properly called Son, the Word who also was with Him and was begotten before the works, when at first He created and arranged all things by Him, is called Christ
translator: Marcus Dods and George Reith (ANF vol. 1)
edition: Jena: F. Mauke, 1842 (Otto ed., vol. 1; Greek with Latin notes; Internet Archive scan bib_fict_4102644_1); Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 as transcribed on newadvent.org (print edition not checked)
what_it_says: The Son, who alone is properly called Son, is the Logos who was with the Father and was begotten before the creatures, when he first created and ordered all things through him.
limits: The text uses the temporal phrase 'before the creatures' and a 'when' clause (ὅτε). It does not say the begetting is eternal or non-temporal, and 2 Apol. gives no further explanation. Arians and Unitarians cite exactly this wording; Otto's note reads ὅτε as quum, not quoniam, and refers the 'with' to Dial. 62.

greek: Χριστὸς μὲν κατὰ τὸ κεχρῖσθαι καὶ κοσμῆσαι τὰ πάντα δι᾽ αὐτοῦ τὸν θεὸν λέγεται, ὄνομα καὶ αὐτὸ περιέχον ἄγνωστον σημασίαν, ὥσπερ καὶ τὸ θεὸς προσαγόρευμα οὐκ ὄνομά ἐστιν, ἀλλὰ πράγματος δυσεξήγητον ἔμφυτος τῇ φύσει τῶν ἀνθρώπων δόξα.
greek_edition: Otto 1842 vol. 1, read from the PDF page image (pdftoppm, 110-120 dpi) and cross-checked with the OCR text layer; OCR-era accents on function words not independently checked. Note: the line in the image reads 'ἀλλὰ πρά-γματος'; I have printed it as πράγματος.
english: is called Christ, in reference to His being anointed and God's ordering all things through Him; this name itself also containing an unknown significance; as also the appellation God is not a name, but an opinion implanted in the nature of men of a thing that can hardly be explained
translator: Marcus Dods and George Reith (ANF vol. 1)
edition: Jena: F. Mauke, 1842 (Otto ed., vol. 1; Greek with Latin notes; Internet Archive scan bib_fict_4102644_1); Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 as transcribed on newadvent.org (print edition not checked)
what_it_says: 'Christ' names the Logos as anointed, through whom God orders all things; the word 'God' is likewise not a name but an innate notion.
limits: Creation is said to be 'through Him' (δι᾽ αὐτοῦ), which is instrumental. Justin does not call him God here; 'God' is glossed as an innate opinion, not a name for the Son.

greek: Ὄνομα δὲ τῷ πάντων πατρὶ θετόν, ἀγεννήτῳ ὄντι, οὔκ ἔστιν· ᾧ γὰρ ἂν καὶ ὀνόματι προσαγορεύηται, πρεσβύτερον ἔχει τὸν θέμενον τὸ ὄνομα. Τὸ δὲ πατὴρ καὶ θεὸς καὶ κτίστης καὶ κύριος καὶ δεσπότης οὐκ ὀνόματά ἐστιν, ἀλλ᾽ ἐκ τῶν εὐποιΐων καὶ τῶν ἔργων προσρήσεις.
greek_edition: Otto 1842 vol. 1, read from the PDF page image (pdftoppm, 110-120 dpi) and cross-checked with the OCR text layer; OCR-era accents on function words not independently checked. 'εὐποιΐων' is read from the image; the OCR text layer has 'εὐποιζῶν'.
english: But to the Father of all, who is unbegotten there is no name given. For by whatever name He be called, He has as His elder the person who gives Him the name. But these words Father, and God, and Creator, and Lord, and Master, are not names, but appellations derived from His good deeds and functions.
translator: Marcus Dods and George Reith (ANF vol. 1)
edition: Jena: F. Mauke, 1842 (Otto ed., vol. 1; Greek with Latin notes; Internet Archive scan bib_fict_4102644_1); Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 as transcribed on newadvent.org (print edition not checked)
what_it_says: The unbegotten Father has no name; any name given to him implies a namer who is older, and words such as Father, God, Creator are descriptions from his works.
limits: Opponents read 'has as His elder the person who gives Him the name' as a claim that the Father is older than the Son. The sentence is general (about any named being) and does not mention the Son or the Logos; it still shows Justin's view that the Father is unbegotten and that the Father's name is not a true name.

greek: Καὶ γὰρ καὶ ἄνθρωπος, ὡς προέφημεν, γέγονε κατὰ τὴν τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ πατρὸς βουλὴν ἀποκυηθεὶς ὑπὲρ τῶν πιστευόντων ἀνθρώπων καὶ ἐπὶ καταλύσει τῶν δαιμόνων.
greek_edition: Otto 1842 vol. 1, read from the PDF page image (pdftoppm, 110-120 dpi) and cross-checked with the OCR text layer; OCR-era accents on function words not independently checked
english: For He was made man also, as we before said, having been conceived according to the will of God the Father, for the sake of believing men, and for the destruction of the demons.
translator: Marcus Dods and George Reith (ANF vol. 1)
edition: Jena: F. Mauke, 1842 (Otto ed., vol. 1; Greek with Latin notes; Internet Archive scan bib_fict_4102644_1); Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 as transcribed on newadvent.org (print edition not checked)
what_it_says: The Son became man by the will of God the Father, for believers and against the demons.
limits: The will of the Father is the cause of the incarnation (γέγονε κατὰ τὴν ... βουλήν). It shows an active will, not that the Son is equal in will or nature. Compare the 'power and will' wording in Dial. 61-62 (not checked here).

greek: Καὶ τοὺς ἀπὸ τῶν Στωϊκῶν δὲ δογμάτων, ἐπειδὴ κἂν τὸν ἠθικὸν λόγον κόσμιοι γεγόνασιν, ὡς καὶ ἔν τισιν οἱ ποιηταὶ διὰ τὸ ἔμφυτον παντὶ γένει ἀνθρώπων σπέρμα τοῦ λόγου, μεμισῆσθαι καὶ πεφονεῦσθαι οἴδαμεν·
greek_edition: Otto 1842 vol. 1, read from the PDF page image (pdftoppm, 110-120 dpi) and cross-checked with the OCR text layer; OCR-era accents on function words not independently checked
english: on account of the seed of reason [the Logos] implanted in every race of men
translator: Marcus Dods and George Reith (ANF vol. 1)
edition: Jena: F. Mauke, 1842 (Otto ed., vol. 1; Greek with Latin notes; Internet Archive scan bib_fict_4102644_1); Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 as transcribed on newadvent.org (print edition not checked)
what_it_says: Stoics and poets were good in their moral teaching because of the seed of the Logos implanted in every race of men, and they were hated for it.
limits: This is the 'Logos spermatikos' passage. The bracket '[the Logos]' is the ANF translator's addition, but the Greek has σπέρμα τοῦ λόγου. It says the seed is implanted in all men; it does not say all men partake of the Logos as Christ (see J3-14 for the phrase the brief attributed to 2 Apol.).

greek: ἀλλὰ κατὰ τὴν τοῦ παντὸς λόγου, ὅ ἐστι Χριστοῦ, γνῶσιν καὶ θεωρίαν πολὺ μᾶλλον μισεῖσθαι οἱ δαίμονες ἐλεγχόμενοι ἐνεργοῦσιν· οἳ τὴν ἀξίαν κόλασιν καὶ τιμωρίαν κομίσονται ἐν αἰωνίῳ πυρὶ ἐγκλεισθέντες.
greek_edition: Otto 1842 vol. 1, read from the PDF page image (pdftoppm, 110-120 dpi) and cross-checked with the OCR text layer; OCR-era accents on function words not independently checked. Otto's note: Perionius conjectured ὃς ἐστι Χριστός; Otto keeps ὅ ἐστι.
english: but by the knowledge and contemplation of the whole Word, which is Christ.
translator: Marcus Dods and George Reith (ANF vol. 1)
edition: Jena: F. Mauke, 1842 (Otto ed., vol. 1; Greek with Latin notes; Internet Archive scan bib_fict_4102644_1); Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 as transcribed on newadvent.org (print edition not checked)
what_it_says: Those who know the whole Word, which is Christ, are hated by the demons more than those who know only a part of the Word.
limits: The identification 'the whole Word, which is Christ' is explicit, but the Greek phrase is ὅ ἐστι (neuter) in the printed text, not ὃς. The passage speaks of knowledge of the Word, not of worship of the Son.

greek: Μεγαλειότερα μὲν οὖν πάσης ἀνθρωπείου διδασκαλίας φαίνεται τὰ ἡμέτερα διὰ τὸ λογικὸν τὸ ὅλον τὸν φανέντα δι᾽ ἡμᾶς Χριστὸν γεγονέναι, καὶ σῶμα καὶ λόγον καὶ ψυχήν.
greek_edition: Otto 1842 vol. 1, read from the PDF page image (pdftoppm, 110-120 dpi) and cross-checked with the OCR text layer; OCR-era accents on function words not independently checked. The Greek begins on p. 304 (image checked).
english: Our doctrines, then, appear to be greater than all human teaching; because Christ, who appeared for our sakes, became the whole rational being, both body, and reason, and soul.
translator: Marcus Dods and George Reith (ANF vol. 1)
edition: Jena: F. Mauke, 1842 (Otto ed., vol. 1; Greek with Latin notes; Internet Archive scan bib_fict_4102644_1); Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 as transcribed on newadvent.org (print edition not checked)
what_it_says: Christian teaching is superior because Christ, who appeared for us, became the whole rational being: body, reason and soul.
limits: This describes the incarnation of the Logos as a complete human being. It does not make the Logos a second deity or define the Trinity; it is a hard passage for those who read Logos only as impersonal reason.

greek: Ὅσα γὰρ καλῶς ἀεὶ ἐφθέγξαντο καὶ εὗρον οἱ φιλοσοφήσαντες ἢ νομοθετήσαντες, κατὰ λόγου μέρος εὑρέσεως καὶ θεωρίας ἐστὶ πονηθέντα αὐτοῖς. Ἐπειδὴ δὲ οὐ πάντα τὰ τοῦ λόγου ἐγνώρισαν, ὅς ἐστι Χριστός, καὶ ἐναντία ἑαυτοῖς πολλάκις εἶπον.
greek_edition: Otto 1842 vol. 1, read from the PDF page image (pdftoppm, 110-120 dpi) and cross-checked with the OCR text layer; OCR-era accents on function words not independently checked
english: For whatever either lawgivers or philosophers uttered well, they elaborated by finding and contemplating some part of the Word. But since they did not know the whole of the Word, which is Christ, they often contradicted themselves.
translator: Marcus Dods and George Reith (ANF vol. 1)
edition: Jena: F. Mauke, 1842 (Otto ed., vol. 1; Greek with Latin notes; Internet Archive scan bib_fict_4102644_1); Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 as transcribed on newadvent.org (print edition not checked)
what_it_says: Philosophers and lawgivers spoke well by knowing part of the Word; because they did not know the whole Word, which is Christ, they contradicted themselves.
limits: Only 'the whole of the Word, which is Christ' is said to be the full knowledge; the Greek does not say the partial Logos is a separate being.

greek: Χριστῷ δέ, τῷ καὶ ὑπὸ Σωκράτους ἀπὸ μέρους γνωσθέντι (λόγος γὰρ ἦν καὶ ἔστιν ὁ ἐν παντὶ ὤν, καὶ διὰ τῶν προφητῶν προειπὼν τὰ μέλλοντα γίνεσθαι καὶ δι᾽ ἑαυτοῦ ὁμοιοπαθοῦς γενομένου καὶ διδάξαντος ταῦτα), οὐ φιλόσοφοι οὐδὲ φιλόλογοι μόνον ἐπείσθησαν
greek_edition: Otto 1842 vol. 1, read from the PDF page image (pdftoppm, 110-120 dpi) and cross-checked with the OCR text layer; OCR-era accents on function words not independently checked. The Greek runs from p. 304 (γνω-) to p. 306 (σθέντι). Image checked on both pages.
english: for He was and is the Word who is in every man, and who foretold the things that were to come to pass both through the prophets and in His own person when He was made of like passions, and taught these things
translator: Marcus Dods and George Reith (ANF vol. 1)
edition: Jena: F. Mauke, 1842 (Otto ed., vol. 1; Greek with Latin notes; Internet Archive scan bib_fict_4102644_1); Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 as transcribed on newadvent.org (print edition not checked)
what_it_says: Christ, partly known even to Socrates, is 'the Word who is in every man', who spoke through the prophets and taught as a man of like passions.
limits: The phrase 'in every man' (ὁ ἐν παντὶ ὤν) is Justin's own; the Greek does not use the verb 'partake' (μετέχω) here (for that wording see J3-14, 1 Apology). The Logos is 'in every man' in the sense of presence; it does not say every man is a Christian.

greek: ἀλλὰ καὶ τεχνῖται καὶ παντελῶς ἰδιῶται καὶ δόξης καὶ φόβου καὶ θανάτου καταφρονήσαντες· ἐπειδὴ δύναμίς ἐστι τοῦ ἀῤῥήτου πατρὸς καὶ οὐχὶ ἀνθρωπείου λόγου κατασκευή.
greek_edition: Otto 1842 vol. 1, read from the PDF page image (pdftoppm, 110-120 dpi) and cross-checked with the OCR text layer; OCR-era accents on function words not independently checked. Page 306 (image checked).
english: since He is a power of the ineffable Father, not the mere instrument of human reason.
translator: Marcus Dods and George Reith (ANF vol. 1)
edition: Jena: F. Mauke, 1842 (Otto ed., vol. 1; Greek with Latin notes; Internet Archive scan bib_fict_4102644_1); Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 as transcribed on newadvent.org (print edition not checked)
what_it_says: Christ is 'a power of the ineffable Father', which is why even craftsmen and the uneducated followed him fearlessly.
limits: This is the brief's 'power' problem: δύναμις is applied to Christ. The 2 Apol. text itself does not name the Holy Spirit (no 'Holy Spirit' or 'prophetic Spirit' in the Greek or ANF English of 2 Apol.). Opponents read 'power' as an impersonal force; the sentence itself contrasts him with human reason. Comparison with the Spirit wording in other works not checked here.

greek: Χριστιανὸς εὑρεθῆναι καὶ εὐχόμενος καὶ παμμάχως ἀγωνιζόμενος ὁμολογῶ οὐχ ὅτι ἀλλότρια ἐστὶ τὰ Πλάτωνος διδάγματα τοῦ Χριστοῦ, ἀλλ᾽ ὅτι οὐκ ἔστι πάντῃ ὅμοια, ὥσπερ οὐδὲ τὰ τῶν ἄλλων, Στωϊκῶν τε καὶ ποιητῶν καὶ συγγραφέων. Ἕκαστος γάρ τις ἀπὸ μέρους τοῦ σπερματικοῦ λόγου τὸ συγγενὲς ὁρῶν καλῶς ἐφθέγξατο.
greek_edition: Otto 1842 vol. 1, read from the PDF page image (pdftoppm, 110-120 dpi) and cross-checked with the OCR text layer; OCR-era accents on function words not independently checked. Otto's note: 'Συγγενές, nimirum σπερματικοῦ λόγου'.
english: For each man spoke well in proportion to the share he had of the spermatic word, seeing what was related to it.
translator: Marcus Dods and George Reith (ANF vol. 1)
edition: Jena: F. Mauke, 1842 (Otto ed., vol. 1; Greek with Latin notes; Internet Archive scan bib_fict_4102644_1); Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 as transcribed on newadvent.org (print edition not checked)
what_it_says: Each thinker spoke well to the extent that he saw what was akin to him in part of the spermatic Logos.
limits: The phrase is 'spermatic word' (σπερματικοῦ λόγου). The English 'in proportion to the share' corresponds to ἀπὸ μέρους. Justin says Plato is not wholly alien to Christ, but also that Plato is not wholly like him; this is not a claim that Plato was a Christian.

greek: Ὅσα οὖν παρὰ πᾶσι καλῶς εἴρηται, ἡμῶν τῶν Χριστιανῶν ἐστί· τὸν γὰρ ἀπὸ ἀγεννήτου καὶ ἀῤῥήτου θεοῦ λόγον μετὰ τὸν θεὸν προσκυνοῦμεν καὶ ἀγαπῶμεν, ἐπειδὴ καὶ δι᾽ ἡμᾶς ἄνθρωπος γέγονεν, ὅπως καὶ τῶν παθῶν τῶν ἡμετέρων συμμέτοχος γενόμενος καὶ ἴασιν ποιήσηται.
greek_edition: Otto 1842 vol. 1, read from the PDF page image (pdftoppm, 110-120 dpi) and cross-checked with the OCR text layer; OCR-era accents on function words not independently checked. Page 312 (image checked).
english: Whatever things were rightly said among all men, are the property of us Christians. For next to God, we worship and love the Word who is from the unbegotten and ineffable God, since also He became man for our sakes, that becoming a partaker of our sufferings, He might also bring us healing.
translator: Marcus Dods and George Reith (ANF vol. 1)
edition: Jena: F. Mauke, 1842 (Otto ed., vol. 1; Greek with Latin notes; Internet Archive scan bib_fict_4102644_1); Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 as transcribed on newadvent.org (print edition not checked)
what_it_says: Christians worship and love the Word, who comes from the unbegotten and ineffable God, next to God; he became man to share our sufferings and heal us.
limits: The Greek μετὰ τὸν θεὸν means 'after God' in order, so the Word is worshipped but placed second; the passage does not use 'God' of the Word or 'homoousios'. It is the strongest 2 Apol. text for worship of the Logos (the brief's item 6), but it is not an explicit claim of equal worship.

greek: Οἱ γὰρ συγγραφεῖς πάντες διὰ τῆς ἐνούσης ἐμφύτου τοῦ λόγου σπορᾶς ἀμυδρῶς ἐδύναντο ὁρᾶν τὰ ὄντα. Ἕτερον γάρ ἐστι σπέρμα τινὸς καὶ μίμημα κατὰ δύναμιν δοθὲν καὶ ἕτερον αὐτό, οὗ κατὰ χάριν τὴν ἀπ᾽ ἐκείνου ἡ μετουσία καὶ μίμησις γίνεται.
greek_edition: Otto 1842 vol. 1, read from the PDF page image (pdftoppm, 110-120 dpi) and cross-checked with the OCR text layer; OCR-era accents on function words not independently checked. Page 312 (image checked).
english: For all the writers were able to see realities darkly through the sowing of the implanted word that was in them. For the seed and imitation impacted according to capacity is one thing, and quite another is the thing itself, of which there is the participation and imitation according to the grace which is from Him.
translator: Marcus Dods and George Reith (ANF vol. 1)
edition: Jena: F. Mauke, 1842 (Otto ed., vol. 1; Greek with Latin notes; Internet Archive scan bib_fict_4102644_1); Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 as transcribed on newadvent.org (print edition not checked)
what_it_says: The writers saw realities darkly through the implanted sowing of the Logos; the seed given according to capacity is different from the thing itself, in which participation is by grace.
limits: This separates the seminal Logos in men from the Logos itself. It is the answer to the claim that Justin's Logos-seed is merely human reason; it is not a full doctrine of the Son's eternal relation to the Father.

ref: 1 Apol. 46.2 (cross-reference: the brief attributed this phrase to 2 Apol.; it is not in 2 Apol.)
greek: Τὸν Χριστὸν πρωτότοκον τοῦ θεοῦ εἶναι ἐδιδάχθημεν καὶ προεμηνύσαμεν λόγον ὄντα, οὗ πᾶν γένος ἀνθρώπων μετέσχε. Καὶ οἳ μετὰ λόγου βιώσαντες Χριστιανοί εἰσι, κἂν ἄθεοι ἐνομίσθησαν
greek_edition: Otto 1842 vol. 1, p. 230 (PDF p. 310), OCR text layer only; not checked against the page image. Mark PARTLY.
english: We have been taught that Christ is the first-born of God, and we have declared above that He is the Word of whom every race of men were partakers
translator: Marcus Dods and George Reith (ANF vol. 1)
edition: Jena: F. Mauke, 1842 (Otto ed., vol. 1; Greek with Latin notes; Internet Archive scan bib_fict_4102644_1); Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 as transcribed on newadvent.org (print edition not checked)
what_it_says: Christ, the first-born of God, is the Logos of whom every race of men partook; those who lived with the Logos are Christians even if called atheists (Socrates, Heraclitus).
limits: This is the phrase the brief attributed to 2 Apol. It is in 1 Apol. 46 (Otto p. 230 / ANF ch. 46), and is not in 2 Apol. The 2 Apol. parallel is J3-09 ('the Word who is in every man'), which does not use μετέχω. The Greek here is from the OCR text layer only (PARTLY).

ref: 2 Apol. 6 (Otto editorial note on the Greek verb)
greek: Sed γεννᾶσθαι est Justino verbum solemne, quo demonstret, λόγον, qui una aderat cum Deo nimirum tamquam attributum divinum (συνὼν sc. τῷ πατρί [Dial. c. Tr. c. 62. p. 285. E: πρὸ πάντ. τ. ποιημ. συννὴν τῷ πατρί])
greek_edition: Otto 1842 vol. 1, note 2 on p. 296 (PDF p. 376), read from the page image. Latin editorial note, not Justin.
edition: Jena: F. Mauke, 1842 (Otto ed., vol. 1; Greek with Latin notes; Internet Archive scan bib_fict_4102644_1)
what_it_says: Otto's note: γεννᾶσθαι is Justin's standard verb for the Logos who was with God, and he cites Dial. 62 for the same 'before all creatures, with the Father' wording; the note also distinguishes ante mundi creationem and λόγος προφορικός (ἐνδιάθετος / προφορικός).
limits: This is a 19th-century editor's note, not evidence of Justin's intent. It points to Dial. 62 (not checked here). The note's Stoic-style distinction (ενδιάθετος / προφορικός) is an editor's reading. Other scholars differ (not checked).
